pll2d4c1-d1e3514.summary: Asks whether God created the angels perfect and blessed or miserable and imperfect.

pll2d4c1-d1e3517.summary: Answers that they were created neither blessed nor miserable: not miserable, since misery comes from sin; and the fallen were never blessed, being ignorant of their future sin and punishment. Had they foreknown it, they would either have wished to avoid it and could not (miserable) or could and would not (foolish and wicked).
claims: Angels were created neither blessed nor miserable.
The fallen did not foreknow their fall.

pll2d4c1-d1e3520.summary: Notes that the good who stood perhaps foreknew their beatitude, citing Augustine on Genesis: perhaps God did not reveal to the devil what he would do or suffer, but revealed to the others that they would remain in the truth.
claims: Perhaps the good angels foreknew their perseverance.

pll2d4c1-d1e3541.summary: Interprets Augustine as suggesting the fallen were never blessed, while those who stood foreknew their beatitude and were in a way blessed by certain hope.
claims: On this view the good angels were blessed by certain hope.

pll2d4c1-d1e3549.summary: Notes that Augustine says this as opinion and inquiry rather than assertion, and objects to it: why would God reveal their future to some and not others, since he does not punish before sin? This suggests he revealed neither future evil nor future good, so neither fallen nor standing angels were blessed until confirmation.
claims: Augustine's suggestion was tentative.
God does not punish the innocent.
Perhaps no angels were blessed before confirmation.

pll2d4c1-d1e3564.summary: Cites Augustine: to say angels could be blessed while uncertain of damnation or salvation is too presumptuous; how can those uncertain of their beatitude be blessed?
claims: Beatitude requires certainty of one's state.

pll2d4c1-d1e3588.summary: Concludes that the fallen were never blessed, unless beatitude means their state of innocence; those who stood either foreknew their future beatitude and were blessed in hope, or were uncertain and not otherwise blessed than the rest. The latter seems more probable to Lombard.
claims: The fallen were never blessed.
More probably the good were also not blessed before confirmation.

pll2d4c1-d1e3591.summary: Answers whether angels were created perfect: in one way perfect, in another imperfect, since 'perfect' is said in several ways.
claims: Angels were perfect in one sense and imperfect in another.

pll2d4c1-d1e3595.summary: Distinguishes three perfections: by time, having all fitting to the time (angels before fall or confirmation); by nature, having all due to the nature for glorification (angels after confirmation, saints after resurrection); and universal, lacking nothing and source of all good (God alone). The first belongs to created nature, the second to glorified nature, the third to uncreated nature.
claims: Perfection is by time, by nature, or universal.
Universal perfection belongs to God alone.

pll2d4c1-d1e3609.summary: Summarizes: the angels at creation were good, not evil; just, that is innocent; perfect in one way and imperfect in another; not blessed until confirmation, unless beatitude means their state of innocence and goodness.
claims: Angels were created good, innocent, partly perfect, and not yet blessed.

pl-l2d4c1.summary: Asks whether angels were created perfect and blessed or miserable and imperfect. They were created neither blessed nor miserable: not miserable, since misery comes from sin; not blessed, for the fallen did not foreknow their fall (if they had, they would have been either miserable or wicked). Augustine suggests the good may have foreknown their beatitude, but this he says as conjecture, and he also asks why God would have revealed the future to some and not others, since he does not punish before sin; and he calls it presumption to call angels blessed if uncertain of their state. Lombard finds more probable that the good too were uncertain and so not blessed before confirmation, unless 'beatitude' means their state of innocence. They were perfect in one sense and imperfect in another: perfection by time (fitting their time), by nature (glorified, after confirmation), and universal (God's alone).
claims: Angels were created neither blessed nor miserable.
Misery comes only from sin.
The fallen angels did not foreknow their fall.
Augustine's suggestion that the good foreknew their beatitude was conjectural.
More probably no angels were blessed before confirmation, unless innocence is called beatitude.
Perfection is threefold: by time, by nature (glorified), and universal (God's alone).
Angels were perfect by time before confirmation, and by nature after it.
